questionText:
A skydiver of mass 76 kg is falling vertically in still air. At time t = 0, the skydiver opens his parachute.

(a) Using Fig. 1.1, determine:
  (i) the deceleration of the skydiver immediately after the parachute opens
  (ii) the force due to air resistance acting on the skydiver immediately after the parachute opens.

(b) Explain, in terms of the forces acting on the skydiver, his motion between t = 0 and t = 6.0 s.

(c) Explain why opening the parachute cannot reduce the speed of the skydiver to zero.
markScheme:
(a)(i) deceleration = any value from 35 to 43 m/s²
(a)(ii) force = 3800 N
(b) Upward force is greater than weight at first, so he decelerates; air resistance decreases as speed decreases, so the deceleration decreases; eventually weight equals air resistance and he reaches terminal/constant velocity.
(c) At zero speed there is no air resistance; weight still acts downward, so there would be a resultant downward force. Equivalently, the forces balance only at a speed greater than zero, so speed cannot decrease to zero once forces balance.

questionText:
(a) Explain, in terms of molecules, why liquids are very difficult to compress.

(b) Fig. 3.1 shows a device that uses liquid pressure to lift heavy boxes. The boxes are lifted by pumping oil into the cylinder. The force upwards on the piston due to the oil, and the force downwards on the piston due to the air above the piston, combine to produce a constant force of 8800 N. The pressure of the air is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the cross-sectional area of the bottom surface of the piston is 0.016 m².
  (i) Calculate the pressure of the oil at the bottom surface of the piston.
  (ii) As the boxes are lifted, the depth of the oil increases. Explain why the pump must exert an increasing pressure on the oil as the depth of the oil increases.
  (iii) Suggest one reason why the force of 8800 N in (b) cannot lift boxes of weight 8800 N.
markScheme:
(a) Molecules are already very close/touching, so the repulsive forces become very large.
(b)(i) pressure = 6.5 × 10⁵ Pa
(b)(ii) Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, so the pump must provide extra pressure to keep the upward force constant / to counteract the increased pressure, force or weight of the oil.
(b)(iii) The initial force must be greater than 8800 N to start motion; or the upward force only balances the weight; or piston/oil weight or friction prevents lifting.

questionText:
An aluminium saucepan with a plastic handle contains cold water. Fig. 4.1 shows the saucepan on a hotplate.

(a) State why the pan is made from aluminium but the handle is made from plastic.

(b) The hotplate is switched on and, as the temperature of the water increases, the internal energy of the water increases.
  (i) State, in terms of molecules, what is meant by an increase in internal energy.
  (ii) Explain, in terms of the atomic lattice and electrons, how thermal energy is transferred through the aluminium.
  (iii) Eventually, the water reaches boiling point. Thermal energy from the hotplate is still being transferred to the water. Explain, in terms of molecules, the effect of this thermal energy on the water.
  (iv) The mass of the water decreases by 0.11 kg in 300 s. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg. Calculate the rate at which the water gains thermal energy.
markScheme:
(a) Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, while plastic is a poor conductor / does not conduct heat.
(b)(i) An increase in internal energy means an increase in the kinetic energy of molecules or an increase in the potential energy of molecules.
(b)(ii) Atoms / lattice vibrate faster; they pass energy to neighbouring atoms by collisions; atoms pass energy to electrons; electrons move through the lattice and hit distant atoms.
(b)(iii) Molecules escape from the liquid as vapour; bonds are broken / attractive forces overcome; molecules gain potential energy / work is done separating molecules.
(b)(iv) rate of gain of energy = 840 W.

questionText:
Fig. 5.1 shows the structure of a liquid-in-glass thermometer. The bulb of the thermometer is placed into a beaker of warm water. As the liquid expands, it moves along the tube.

(a) Explain, in terms of molecules, why a liquid expands when heated.

(b) Explain, in terms of molecules, why a liquid expands more than a solid when heated.

(c) A second thermometer has a larger bulb that contains more of the same liquid than the thermometer shown in Fig. 5.1. It has a different scale. In every other way, it is identical.
  (i) Explain how the sensitivity of the second thermometer compares with the sensitivity of the thermometer in Fig. 5.1.
  (ii) Explain how the range of the second thermometer compares with the range of the thermometer in Fig. 5.1.

(d)
  (i) State one everyday problem that is a result of thermal expansion.
  (ii) Suggest and explain one way of solving this problem.
markScheme:
(a) Molecules gain kinetic energy / speed up; molecules move further apart or push others away.
(b) Forces between liquid molecules are weaker than in solids; less energy/work is needed to separate molecules.
(c)(i) Greater sensitivity, because the larger bulb gives a greater volume increase and the liquid moves a greater distance for the same temperature increase.
(c)(ii) Smaller range, because the liquid reaches the end of the tube after a smaller temperature increase / greater sensitivity in the same tube length.
(d)(i) Example: bridges buckle in hot weather.
(d)(ii) Example solution: allow gaps / expansion joints so the bridge can expand and the gaps close.

markScheme:

• interaction / overlap between the (magnetic) fields of the magnets and the coil;
• this produces a force on (each side of) the coil;
